clue.text: So Kipling's great steamers, travelling world incognito: not a hundred left or scuttled

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to take the following item away from the long phrase before it
a scuttled ship is wrecked and broken up, so the gathered letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, the raw letters to work on
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred; it is removed
L is the usual abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: Liners steam round the world unrecognised, while a hundred others are left behind or sunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's Just So verse runs: 'the steamers white and gold go rolling down to Rio'. Drop C from WORLD INCOGNITO, add L and OR, and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is quoted from Kipling's verse describing how the big ships voyage south to Brazil's famous port.

clue.text: Frost's poem, the Ancient Mariner?

blocks.note: first meaning: hoar frost, ice crystals on surfaces
second meaning: Coleridge's poem title begins with this word

explanation.walkthrough: The capital makes 'Frost' look like the poet Robert Frost, but it is plain frozen dew; the poem is Coleridge's, not his.
explanation.definitionFit: Rime is feathery ice deposited from fog, and Coleridge's ballad is titled The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.

clue.text: Some bowlers aim to wreck: oblige feet to move

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for what some bowlers aim at

indicators.note: making the letters move shifts them out of their printed order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Bowlers set out to destroy the batsman's stumps by forcing his feet to shift.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, leg before wicket (lbw) is a way of getting a batsman out when the ball hits his leg in front of the stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Many cricket bowlers deliberately target the pads, hoping the umpire will give the batsman out lbw.

clue.text: Work up? Nice work - if you can get it!

indicators.note: to work something is to knead and reshape it, so its letters change places

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The old song line: nice work if you can get it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice work if you can get it' is a Gershwin song title, which hides that 'work' is the instruction here.
explanation.definitionFit: To incite people is to stir or rouse them into action, which is what working them up means.

clue.text: Appliance of modern-day force: get out of it!

blocks.note: g is the symbol for gravitational force
AD, anno Domini, labels the present era
taken as written

explanation.surface: A device belonging to the modern police is told to clear off.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadget is a small mechanical or electronic device, a handy contraption or tool.

clue.text: Panda car crashing during tour of duty

indicators.note: a crashing vehicle is smashed up, so its letters are jumbled
'during' puts one thing within the span of another, so it sits inside

blocks.note: the three letters rearranged
a police officer's beat is the round patrolled on duty

explanation.surface: A police patrol car smashes up while officers are out on their round.
explanation.walkthrough: A panda car is British slang for a small police patrol car, so the surface pulls 'Panda' into it; the animal alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bearcat is another name for the red panda, the small reddish tree-dwelling mammal of the Himalayas.

clue.text: Rued looking up Miss Smith's recipe network

indicators.note: in a down entry, looking up means the letters run from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: Delia Smith is a famous British television cook
the web is a network; with Delia it suggests her recipe website

explanation.surface: Someone regrets browsing a celebrity cook's online collection of recipes.
explanation.walkthrough: Delia Smith is a well-known British cookery writer; her name and WEB are written bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewail something is to lament it, voicing grief or regret, as when one rues a loss.

clue.text: Right! Name a beast evolving from the aardvarks

indicators.note: evolving things change form over time, so the letters develop into a new order

blocks.note: R is the usual abbreviation for right
N is the abbreviation for name
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An exclamation as a creature is named that descended from aardvarks.
explanation.definitionFit: Antbear is an alternative name for the aardvark, the burrowing African termite-eater.

clue.text: Joyce who wrote: "Work hard, raise a City partner and point to a growing family"

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising letters lifts them so they read from bottom to top

blocks.note: Joyce Cary was an English novelist
op, short for opus, is a work
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
taken as written
EC is the postcode of the City of London
an ally is a partner
E, east, is a compass point

explanation.surface: A writer's motto quoted: toil, promote a business partner and aim at a growing household.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at James Joyce, but the author is Joyce Cary. A, EC and ALLY are reversed together to give YLLACEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Caryophyllaceae is the botanical family of pinks and carnations, so a family of growing plants.

clue.text: H-horned characters, perhaps, get around this barrier

indicators.note: letters moved around are shifted out of their order into a new one

blocks.note: the characters, or letters, of the word as printed
taken as written

explanation.surface: Animals with horns try to find a way round an obstacle.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorn hedge is a living fence of prickly shrubs such as hawthorn, planted to keep livestock in or out.

clue.text: Soldier wearing waterproof: that's charming!

indicators.note: a person wearing a coat is inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: GI is an American soldier
a mac, short for mackintosh, is a British raincoat

explanation.surface: A soldier in a raincoat earns an ironic compliment.
explanation.walkthrough: A mac is a British name for a raincoat.
explanation.definitionFit: Magic as an exclamation is British slang for wonderful, just as 'that's charming!' expresses delight.

clue.text: See 1
It's Hoddle with we ten, sadly: so what did the eleventh do?

definitions.text: so what did the eleventh do?
definitions.note: a question whose reply is the verb phrase

indicators.note: something sadly done is badly done, so the letters end up disordered

blocks.note: taken as written apart from 'with', which only joins

explanation.surface: A football squad laments that Hoddle is left with just ten players and asks what the missing man did.
explanation.walkthrough: Glenn Hoddle was then England's football manager. A team has eleven players; the absent eleventh let the team down.
explanation.definitionFit: Letting the side down means failing your teammates, the natural reproach for a player who has gone missing.

clue.text: Hitchcockian setting of "O! Let me stab wildly!"

indicators.note: acting wildly means flailing without order, so the letters fly about

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cry from a knife-wielding killer in a Hitchcock thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the famous shower scene in Psycho, which happens at this very motel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bates Motel is where Norman Bates commits his murders in Hitchcock's film Psycho.

clue.text: Jack's address keeps a place for the Old Man

blocks.note: taken as written
the Old Man of Hoy is a sea stack off this Orkney island

explanation.surface: A sailor's home has a spare room for his father.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack, a jack tar, is a sailor; 'address' is a greeting, not a home. The Old Man of Hoy is a famous rock pillar in Scotland's Orkney isles.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors hail other ships or shipmates with this call, so it is how a seaman greets someone.

clue.text: See about charm offensive? Who knows?

indicators.note: an offensive is an attack, and attacked letters are knocked into a new order
'about' means going round, so the first word surrounds the rest

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to look into a campaign of flattery, and shrugs.
explanation.walkthrough: A charm offensive is a concerted effort to win people over, so the phrase reads as one idea.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Search me' is an idiom said with a shrug, meaning I have no idea, the same as asking who knows.

clue.text: Tiny Tim right to get a ticking-off about it

blocks.note: c, short for circa, means about
R is the usual abbreviation for right
taken as written
tch is the clicking noise of disapproval
taken as written

explanation.surface: Little Tim deserves a scolding for something.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'about' block goes first even though it comes late in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny Tim is the sickly youngest son of Bob Cratchit's family in Dickens's A Christmas Carol.

clue.text: Antigone's tragedy no good to such collegians

indicators.note: 'no' means without, so the next item is struck out
a tragedy is a disaster, wrecking the order of the letters

blocks.note: taken as written, the possessive S included
G is the abbreviation for good; it is taken away

explanation.surface: Sophocles' Antigone is no use to a class of schoolboys studying it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tragedy' fits the Greek play perfectly, hiding that it is the instruction. Eton College is an elite English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: Etonians are pupils or old boys of Eton College, which is formally a college, hence collegians.

clue.text: Blackguard and apostate living in old city quarter

indicators.note: someone living in a place is housed inside it, so one piece sits within the others

blocks.note: a rat is a deserter or turncoat
ex means former
EC is the postcode of the City of London
E, east, is one quarter of the compass

explanation.surface: A scoundrel and a turncoat dwell in an ancient district of town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blackguard' looks like a noun for a villain, but it is a verb meaning to abuse verbally.
explanation.definitionFit: To blackguard someone is to revile them in strong language, and to execrate is to curse or denounce.

clue.text: Haul left in robbery

blocks.note: a bag is a haul, the catch taken by a hunter
L is the usual abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: The loot was abandoned during a heist.
explanation.walkthrough: Blag is British criminal slang for a robbery, especially a violent one.
explanation.definitionFit: In British underworld slang a blag is a hold-up or raid, a theft by force.

clue.text: Double blow from the micro-network

blocks.note: first meaning: a boxer's quick pair of punches
second meaning: a joking tiny network made of just stations One and Two, as on BBC radio

explanation.walkthrough: BBC Radio 1 and Radio 2 are British national stations; a network of only those two would be very small indeed.
explanation.definitionFit: In boxing a one-two is a jab followed at once by a cross, two punches in rapid succession.

clue.text: Outstanding work sought in disaster areas

blocks.note: first meaning: sculpture whose figures stand out from a flat background
second meaning: aid such as food and shelter sent to victims

explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' reads as excellent, but it means literally standing out from the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A relief is carved artwork projecting from its ground, and relief is also emergency aid for those in need.

clue.text: The Mr Fixit of the Child Support Agency?

definitions.text: The Mr Fixit of the Child Support Agency?

blocks.note: surface reading: the handyman who repairs things around a building
setter's reading: this agency chased absent fathers for payments towards their children's upkeep, so its typical man is one who pays

explanation.walkthrough: The Child Support Agency was a British government body that made absent parents pay toward their children's keep.
explanation.definitionFit: A handyman doing repairs is called by this name, and an absent father paying child support is one too.

clue.text: Mass circulation impediment

blocks.note: first meaning: a lump of thickened matter
second meaning: a blockage of blood flow in a vessel

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass circulation' looks like a newspaper's big readership; split it after the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: A clot is a coagulated lump of blood that can block an artery and stop the blood flowing.

clue.text: Photograph a man with creativity: might get snap out of it

blocks.note: a take is a shot recorded by a camera
he refers to a man
art is creative skill

explanation.surface: A photographer shoots an artistic man, who may produce a quick picture from it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snap' tempts as a photograph, completing the camera picture, but here it means to recover your spirits abruptly.
explanation.definitionFit: To take heart is to cheer up and regain courage, as one does on shaking off gloom.

clue.text: Faultless banker's self-assertion?

blocks.note: first meaning: perfect
second meaning: in card games the banker hands out the cards, and might announce so in two words

explanation.walkthrough: The banker is the dealer in gambling games like pontoon, so the word splits as I DEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ideal is perfect, matching a standard of excellence with no flaws or defects.

clue.text: Say! Not bad for excellent line one carries

definitions.note: an example of the figure of speech, flagged by 'Say'

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for line
I is the Roman numeral one
to tote is to carry

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that a fine line of verse is merely not bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' means for example: saying 'not bad' when you mean excellent is an instance of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Litotes is understatement made by denying the opposite, as in calling something superb merely not bad.

clue.text: Bohemian syncopation?

blocks.note: first meaning: unconventional, eccentric
second meaning: musical stress placed on the weak pulse

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bohemian' tempts as Czech or as a style of music; it means arty and unconventional.
explanation.definitionFit: Offbeat describes unusual people and tastes, and syncopation is accenting the beats normally left weak.
